c.tagline: Cuba's first city, walled in by El Yunque and the sea, where the cacao rivers run to the Caribbean's wildest coast

card: US-issued credit and debit cards do not work anywhere in Cuba due to the embargo, and this applies fully in Baracoa. Even non-US Visa/Mastercard have almost no acceptance here — Hotel El Castillo and Hotel Porto Santo are the only spots that occasionally process foreign cards, and outages are common. Bring all the cash you'll need for your entire stay; casas particulares, paladares, bici-taxis, and excursions are cash-only.
rides: Private "particular" taxis (classic American cars/Ladas, negotiated fare)
Horse-drawn coches for short local trips

taxi.color: No uniform livery — private taxis are typically unmarked 1950s American classics or Soviet-era Ladas; the rare state Cubataxi is marked with company decals
taxi.fare: $1–3 for a ride across town, $25–35 per person for the shared 5-hour trip to Santiago de Cuba over La Farola
taxi.fareNote: Meters essentially don't exist — always agree on the price in cash before getting in, and confirm whether it's quoted in USD or CUP

emergency.note: Fire brigade is 105. Baracoa's Hospital General Docente 'Ciro Redondo García' handles routine and emergency care, but serious cases are transferred to Santiago de Cuba, roughly 4-5 hours away via La Farola — factor this into any remote hiking or diving plans.

walk: The historic core is small and flat — you can cross it end to end on foot in about 20 minutes along Calle José Martí and the Malecón. Sidewalks are narrow and cobblestones uneven, and street lighting thins out fast once you leave the center, so a flashlight helps after dark.

safety.safety: Baracoa is widely considered one of the safest towns in Cuba for solo travelers — violent crime against visitors is rare and locals are famously welcoming and protective of guests staying in casas particulares.
safety.crime: The real risks are petty and opportunistic: unattended bags on Playa Maguana, unlocked casa windows, and jineteros steering tourists toward commission-paying casas, tours, or overpriced 'guides' for El Yunque. Normal precautions are enough.

hood_landmark.Casco Histórico: Catedral de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción
hood_landmark.El Paraíso: Hotel El Castillo mirador (Castillo de Seboruco)
hood_landmark.Playa de Miel: Río Miel river mouth and black-sand beach
hood_landmark.Zona del Mercado / Terminal: Fuerte de la Punta y el Mercado Agropecuario

avoid.reason: Persistent jinetero touts and overcharging are the main nuisance; keep an eye on belongings on the Malecón at night.

hood_desc: The compact colonial grid around Parque Independencia — Baracoa's oldest streets, the cathedral holding the Cruz de la Parra, and the highest concentration of paladares and casas particulares.
The seafront promenade linking the two old Spanish forts, lined with pastel houses, a scattering of bars and the Casa de la Trova; this is where the whole town turns out at sunset.
A steep residential hillside above downtown, home to Hotel El Castillo's panoramic terrace and quieter casas with sweeping views over the bay and El Yunque.
A short walk south of center, where the Río Miel meets the sea at a black-volcanic-sand beach — a low-key, mostly local spot to swim away from the crowds.
The workaday north end of town near the bus terminal and produce market, with cheaper casas, the Cadeca exchange office, and onward transport to Guantánamo and the airport.

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water, as everywhere in Cuba.

transit.sys: No formal public transit system exists
transit.hours: Informal transport (bici-taxis, coches) runs roughly dawn to 10pm
transit.pay: Cash only, fare negotiated per ride — USD, EUR, or CUP
transit.map: No transit map; the town is small enough to navigate with a basic sketch map from your casa host
transit.note: Getting around means walking, flagging a bici-taxi (about $1 in town), or hiring a horse-cart or private car for excursions like El Yunque or Playa Maguana. There are no buses, metros, or ride-hailing apps of any kind.

transport.air: Gustavo Rizo Airport (BCA), 2 km north of town, has had no reliable scheduled service since Cubana suspended its Havana route in 2018; occasional charter or seasonal Aerogaviota flights appear and disappear, so treat flying as a bonus, not a plan.
transport.train: No rail line reaches Baracoa or anywhere else in eastern Guantánamo province.
transport.bus: Víazul runs a daily coach from Santiago de Cuba via Guantánamo City and La Farola (about 5 hours) plus a long-haul Havana route (16-18 hours); book several days ahead in high season since seats sell out fast.
transport.ferry: No scheduled ferry or boat service connects Baracoa to any other Cuban port.
transport.car: Self-drive or a hired car over La Farola — the dramatic 55 km mountain highway to Guantánamo City, one of Cuba's highest paved roads — is the classic overland route; a shared colectivo taxi covers the same road for roughly $25-35 per person.

airport.name: Gustavo Rizo Airport
airport.distance: 2 km (1.2 mi) north of downtown Baracoa
airport.transport: No fixed shuttle or taxi rank — arrange a private taxi in advance or have your casa host send a driver (roughly $3-5 into town), since flights are infrequent and irregular.

net.m: ETECSA is Cuba's sole mobile carrier; buy a short-term tourist SIM or top up a Nauta account at the ETECSA office near Parque Independencia. 3G/4G works in the town center but drops out quickly once you head toward El Yunque, Maguana, or Yumurí.
net.w: There is no home-style broadband here — even hotel 'wifi' typically runs on the same public Nauta hotspot cards used in the parks, and Hotel El Castillo's signal is often the strongest in town.
net.gb: $1-2/hour for Nauta wifi-hotspot cards; mobile data bundles run roughly $10-30 for a few GB, best bought in advance through the ETECSA app
net.fwn: Nauta wifi-hotspot cards are the closest thing to 'free' wifi and are sold at the ETECSA office or by street resellers; connect at Parque Independencia or the Malecón wifi zones
net.ap: A physical ETECSA/Nauta SIM is essential for foreign phones — there's no roaming onto Cuba's closed network, so buy one at the airport or the ETECSA office and expect to rely on prepaid data or wifi-hotspot cards rather than continuous coverage.

tip.s: 10% for tour guides, hike leaders, and bici-taxi drivers is appreciated; round up small change for casa staff who cook or clean for you.
tip.r: Leave about 10% in cash at paladares and casas particulares — card tipping doesn't exist here, and staff at state-run restaurants rely on tips far more than their official wages.
